South American single origin coffee from Brazil, Colombia and Peru. 8 lots in stock right now. Expect real body, milk chocolate and nuts, soft acidity and a citrus note underneath. Choose your lot and roast level, or let Roaster’s Choice pick for you. Roasted to order on our Buckeye roasters in Concord, California and shipped within 72 hours in 6oz, 12oz, 24oz or 5lb bags.
South American single origin coffee is the comfort food of the coffee world. Good body, gentle acidity, chocolate and nuts, a little citrus around the edges. If you have ever handed someone a cup and watched them relax, odds are it came from Brazil, Colombia or Peru. We have 8 South American single origin coffee lots in stock right now, plus Roaster’s Choice. Every bag on this page is roasted after you order it, at the roast level you choose.
What Makes South American Single Origin Coffee Different
Scale and consistency, mostly. Brazil alone grows about a third of the world’s coffee. The result is a cup with weight to it: heavier body than you get from East Africa, sweeter than Central America, and far less likely to surprise you.
Think milk chocolate rather than dark. Almond, hazelnut, brown sugar, sometimes a soft orange note underneath. Acidity is there but it stays polite, which is exactly why this region ends up in most espresso blends and most office pots. It also means South American single origin coffee is hard to ruin. Slightly off water temperature or a slightly coarse grind will not wreck it.
The exception on this page is the Bob-O-Link program from Fazenda Ambiental Fortaleza in Brazil’s Mogiana region. Those are small natural process lots from individual farms, and they taste more like fruit and wine than a diner cup. They are the reason to look twice at Brazil.
Choosing Your South American Single Origin Coffee: 8 Lots in Stock
This is the current South American single origin coffee inventory at the roastery. Every lot below is in stock and ready to roast.
Brazil
Brazil Cerrado. The workhorse. Low acidity, heavy body, peanut and cocoa. If you want something that tastes like a great diner cup, start here.
Brazil FAF Bob-O-Link Reserve Sitio Sassafrass Natural. A single farm natural from the Bob-O-Link project. Red fruit, chocolate and a syrupy, winey sweetness.
Brazil FAF Bob-O-Link Reserve Serra Dos Ciganos Natural. Higher grown than most of the Mogiana lots. Dried cherry, caramel and a cleaner finish.
Brazil FAF Bob-O-Link Reserve Dirapitinga Natural Yellow. Yellow fruited varieties, dry processed. Honey, apricot and milk chocolate with a soft, rounded body.
Colombia and Peru
Colombia Supremo 17/18. The classic. Balanced, medium bodied, cocoa and walnut with a clean apple brightness.
Colombia Reserva Del Patron. A step up in sweetness and clarity. Caramel, red fruit and a long finish.
Colombia Organic Sierra Nevada FTO. Grown near the Caribbean coast. Lighter, more floral, with citrus and a gentle body.
Peru Warmikuna Women’s Coffee. Grown and processed by women producers in northern Peru. Smooth and sweet with toasted nuts, light cocoa and a mild citrus lift.
Roaster’s Choice. Skip the decision and we will send whatever South American single origin coffee is drinking best on the roaster that week.
Choosing Your Roast Level for South American Single Origin Coffee
Medium is the natural home for this region. It gets you the chocolate and the nuts with enough sweetness left to carry the cup. Nearly every lot above is good at medium.
Light roast is worth it for the three Bob-O-Link naturals, the Sierra Nevada and Reserva Del Patron, where there is fruit and floral character that a longer roast burns off.
Dark roast belongs to Brazil Cerrado. It has the density and the low acidity to take a dark roast without turning ashy, and that is where you get real espresso body. Peru handles a medium dark nicely too. Our guide to choosing the perfect roast covers what each level actually does to the bean.
Roasted to Order in Concord, California
There is a window where roasted coffee is at its best, and it is roughly 7 to 21 days after the roast date. Inside that window the beans have finished degassing but the aromatics are still intact. Outside it, on either side, you are drinking a lesser version of the same coffee.
So we do not stock roasted bags. We roast your South American single origin coffee on Buckeye roasters here in Concord and it leaves within 72 hours. That is how fresh roasted coffee shipped nationwide is supposed to work.
Sizes and Grind
Pick from 6oz, 12oz, 24oz and 5lb. Most single drinkers do well on 12oz at a time. The 5lb is for offices, and if that is you, look at our wholesale program .

Joia rara means “rare jewel” in Portuguese, and this coffee earns the name. It is grown by Sérgio Ricardo Barbosa of the acclaimed Barbosa family. Moreover, it reflects a new generation of excellence in specialty coffee production. One cup makes the case: Fazenda Joia Rara is a gem worth finding.
About Fazenda Joia Rara
The farm lies in the Cerrado, Brazil’s first Denomination of Origin coffee region, where rainy summers and long, dry winters create ideal ripening conditions. The Barbosa name carries weight in Brazilian specialty coffee, and Sérgio represents its next chapter — curious, exacting, and unafraid to experiment. For this lot, he grew Topazio, a Brazilian cultivar known for its sweetness and uniform ripening. Then came the signature move: a controlled 48-hour fermentation before drying. The cherries dry whole afterward, so the fruit’s slow fermentation keeps building flavor inside the bean. As a result, the cup gains vibrant fruit intensity without losing its clean, polished finish.
What’s in the Cup
Rich milk chocolate leads. Next, vibrant red fruit arrives, reminiscent of ripe cherry. Finally, juicy mango brightens the top notes. The body is silky, the sweetness comes in layers, and the finish stays clean. Consequently, this coffee shines as a pour-over, where the fruit unfolds sip by sip. It also makes a chocolate-forward espresso with a fruity twist. Iced, the mango note steals the show. For filter brewing, start with a 1:16 ratio and adjust to taste.
Like all of our microlots , this is a limited harvest — once this lot is gone, it’s gone. Explore the collection for more small-lot discoveries. body: This Fairtrade coffee comes from Codech (Coordinator of Organizations for the Development of Concepcion Huista), located in the department of Huehuetenango in Guatemala and consists of Bourbon, Cattura, Pach, Catuai, and Typica. In 1998, the Alliance for Youth Community Development (ADEJUC in Spanish) arrived at Concepción Huista, Huehuetenango, and began lobbying with the different organizations working in the municipality with the purpose of forming an entity that would represent the social, political, economic, environmental and cultural interests of the municipality. That is how on August 19, 1999, CODECH began. CODECH currently consists of eight grassroots organizations, 6 of these have legal status and two recognized at the municipal level (Municipal organization and Magisterial Council of Women). In total, they account for almost 500 active members: 167 women and 326 men. In 2001, the board of CODECH began to strengthen, participating in training processes at the local, provincial, and national levels, and start to submit proposals for funding to achieve the objectives. In 2003, the Alliance for Community Youth Development financially supports CODECH to implement the comprehensive development program focused on children. During 2004, CODECH received funding from Intermon Oxfam, to manage and execute the project “Coffee and sustainable development for the municipality of Concepcion Huista”. With this project there was support for the small producers to produce and market organic coffee, thus preventing the pollution of the environment, taking rational advantage of the existing resources, and making it easier to enter markets that recognize more favorable and stable prices for the growers. Today, among the eight organizations, 550 hectares of coffee are being cultivated, at an altitude that ranges between 1,500 and 2,032 meters above sea level. 300 Ha of coffee has been certified fair trade (FLO). In addition to the income received by each member, many families have benefited from technical assistance, training processes, and have support with inputs, and improvement in the quality and prices of the coffee. Also, in addition to the income obtained by fair trade (for every 100 pounds sold, a social premium of US $ 10 is received), which is invested in education, health, the functioning of the grassroots organizations, and the functioning of CODECH.

body:
Sidama is a fertile region in southern Ethiopia that spans across the highlands of Lake Awasa in the Rift Valley. The high altitudes that soar beyond 2000 meters above sea level are where Arabica coffee trees grow and ripen slowly in the cool temperatures, resulting in complex flavor profiles and distinct aromas that are characteristic of Sidama green coffee.
The majority of coffee from Ethiopia is natural processed, which requires fewer resources and minimal infrastructure. Only the ripest coffee cherries are harvested and dried whole, usually on patios or raised beds in the sun, allowing for some fermentation. After achieving optimal moisture levels, the cherries are hulled to separate the fruit from the beans. The natural process results in sweet, intense flavors with a strong fruit-forward profile like the sweet strawberry and star fruit notes found in this Sidama G4 coffee.
What We Taste: Notes of black tea lemon grass, with undertones of cocoa powder, brown sugar and golden raisins.

body:
What started as a seasonal espresso blend somehow became one of the most permanent offerings at Odd Box. Pantomime is now our most popular coffee, and for good reason. If you're not sure where to start, this is a pretty darn good place.
Like all of our blends, Pantomime is a blended post-roast. Meaning, we roast each coffee separately, bringing out the characteristics we like most from each one, then blend them together afterward. It gives us much more control over the final flavor and lets us play matchmaker with coffees that might otherwise never meet.
Pantomime leans lighter, but there's enough roast development to put it comfortably in the medium roast camp. As espresso, the Ethiopian component really shines, bringing citrusy notes and crisp acidity to the party. Colombian and Brazilian coffees fill things out with sweet toffee and milk chocolate, giving the whole blend a little more weight and balance.
And if you're a latte person, you're in luck. Those toffee and chocolate notes have enough oomph to push through the dairy, making for a smooth, velvety, ridiculously drinkable cup.
Of course, Pantomime doesn't require an espresso machine. It makes a great drip coffee, too! Because apparently being our most popular espresso blend wasn't enough (overachiever).

The Coffee Review Cupping Notes:
Score: 92.0 Blind Assessment: Sweetly roast-toned, chocolaty. Dark chocolate, lily, vanilla, dried fig, scorched cedar in aroma and cup. Bittersweet-savory structure; crisp yet velvety mouthfeel. Dark chocolate notes lead in the finish, rounding to dried fruit and vanilla notes in the long.
We are proud to report that on The Coffee Review this coffee earned the third-highest rating in a cupping of African Great Lakes coffees for Coffee Review’s June 2021 report. Moreover it earned the distinct motion for a successful dark toast: "Most coffees we test over the course of a year are light-medium to medium in roast, reflecting each individual roaster’s personally calibrated goal of fully developing the character of the bean while leaving behind neither a distracting scorchy edge nor the grassy, nutty hints of an underdeveloped roast. This month, however, we review one successful darker roast, the Valverde Burundi Kinyovu (92; sweetly roast-toned, roundly pungent and chocolaty).
The Coffee Review Notes: This coffee earned a third-highest rating in a cupping of African Great Lakes coffees for Coffee Review’s June 2021 report. Produced by smallholding women farmers near the Kinyovu Washing Station entirely from local strains of the Bourbon variety of Arabica, and processed by the washed method (fruit skin and flesh are removed from the beans before they are dried). Valverde Coffee Roasters is a specialty roaster with locations in Salisbury, Massachusetts and La Paz, Bolivia.
The Coffee Review Bottom Line: An inviting darker-roasted Burundi with deep, rich chocolate notes throughout, complicated by sweet florals, dried fruit, and a pleasingly smoky cedar.
Historically, this coffee was a first-place winner of the coveted Cup of Excellence in 2013. Processed through one of Burundi’s few double fermentation washing stations, Kinyovu coffee cherries are cultivated by women coffee farmers in a high-altitude micro climate, grown among tea, bananas, beans and cassava plants. Through a partnership with a nonprofit organization of women and men in the coffee industry, these farmers receive training on best practices for quality coffee production, from caring for the trees to careful sorting of the ripened cherries during harvest. JNP Coffee pays women farmers a share of the premium for their high-quality coffee earns in the global market. These payments enable new economic opportunities and provide a better quality of life for their families, especially their children.
In 2017, 1,146 farmers under the IWCA Burundi’s program brought cherries at Kinyovu washing station, 1,057 were women and 89 men (also allowed to be part of the program). Thus, 92% of he farmers at Kinyovu are women. The washing station is part of the 21 washing stations under the Sogestal Kayanza umbrella, which is majority owned by private individuals (including Jeanine) with a small percentage remaining under the government ownership (planned to be privatized in the future). Each washing station has an independent general manager and an independent quality manager. The average yearly production of Specialty coffee from Kinyovu is 60,000 kilograms (about three containers) of green export coffee.

Colombia Supremo Huila is grown certified farms by multiple smallholder farmers in the surroundings area of the town of San Agustín, Huila department. Colombia is the largest producer of washed Arabica coffee and third total highest in the world, after Brazil and Vietnam. Its annual production ranges from 12 million to 15 million 70-kilo (154 lbs) bags. Colombia is very unique and is able to produce coffee all 12 months of the year due to it’s range of micro-climates and terrain. In addition, the primary varieties grown in Colombia are Caturra, Bourbon, Typica and Variedad (resistant to leaf rust disease know as Roya). Colombian coffee is referred by the region in which it is grown and altitudes range from 1,200 – 2,000 meters above sea level. Grade: Supremo – Screen 17/18 European Preparation (EP) – Screen 15 Excelso – Screen 14/16. It is without a doubt an excellent coffee that offers great quality and delicious flavor notes of cholocolate, apple and brown sugar.

body:
For years everyone assumed Chiroso was a Caturra mutation. It looks like one — short trees, pale green leaves, and it grows the way Caturra grows. Then the genetics came back Ethiopian. That is the whole coffee in one sentence: it looks Colombian and it drinks like something that wandered in from somewhere else. We cupped this lot and wrote the same word down four times. Juicy . So we bought it.
Alex Metrio farms El Silencio in Urrao, Antioquia, between 1,800 and 1,900 meters. Volcanic ash, cold nights, a lot of rain. Chiroso is a high-altitude specialist — it wants the cool, and Urrao gives it plenty, which is why the variety keeps taking top spots at Cup of Excellence out of exactly this corner of Colombia. Ripe cherry only. Everything else is hand-sorted and floated out at the farm.
Then thirty hours underwater. The cherries ferment submerged and sealed before anything gets pulped, calibrated on Cofinet's protocol to build sweetness and acidity together. Then pulped, the mucilage washed off completely, and ten days on parabolic dryers in thin layers, turned by hand.
We roast it light, far enough that some caramel is built and the lime reads as juice instead of raw acid. Not so far that we bury either one.
In the cup: lime up front, bright and round rather than sharp. Caramel underneath, holding it together. Silky body, sweet the whole way through. Optimal for filter — pour over or drip. It pulls a vivid, fruit-forward espresso too if that's how you drink.
Under 50 bags (12 oz / 340g each). It will not be restocked.
